cultivar: Local Jiuqu population bushes and Longjing-area cultivars such as Longjing 43 and Jiukeng
processing: Fully oxidised small-leaf black: a bud with one or two leaves is withered, rolled tightly into fine hooks, oxidised and dried gently, keeping the leaf whole.
harvest_season: Spring, from around Qingming to Guyu (April), picked as finely as the Longjing next door.
appearance_dry: Fine, tightly curled dark strands bent into little hooks, with a slight sheen.
appearance_liquor: Bright red, clear, the colour that gives the tea its 'red plum' name.
appearance_wet: Small, tender copper-red leaves, very even.
taste_profile: Sweet and smooth with plum and a rose-like floral note, honey underneath and a light body with no rough edges.

brewing.notes: Fine leaf: water around 85–90 °C and short steeps, or it turns tannic. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 2.5 minutes, neat. A glass pot shows the colour.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest only, in small quantities, often with the picking date; best within a year. Production is tiny next to Hangzhou's green tea, so it sells out early and is rarely found abroad.
description:
Jiu Qu Hong Mei is the one black tea Hangzhou makes, from the hills south-west of West Lake in what was Zhoupu township and is now Shuangpu, where every other garden is Longjing. The name means 'red plum of the nine bends': 'nine bends' after the Nine Bend Stream in Wuyi, because the usual account has black-tea skills arriving with Fujian migrants in the nineteenth century, and 'red plum' for the colour of the liquor.

It is made as finely as the green tea around it. A bud with one or two spring leaves is withered, rolled tightly so the leaf curls into small hooks, oxidised and dried gently; the local population bushes and Longjing-area cultivars have small, tender leaves, so the tea is delicate rather than brisk. Whole leaf, fine picking and a short oxidation window are what separate it from a workaday Zhejiang black.

In the cup it is sweet and smooth with plum and a rose-like floral, honey underneath and almost no tannin; the colour is a clear bright red that looks good in glass. It wants gentle treatment – water around 88 °C and short steeps in a gaiwan, or two and a half minutes in a pot – and it rewards being drunk neat. Boiling water and long steeps are what make people say it is thin.

It is sold only as the current spring harvest, by a handful of makers and the Hangzhou tea shops, and the quantity is tiny next to Longjing, so it is seldom exported. Look for fine, evenly hooked dark leaf with a sheen and a sweet, fruity dry smell; coarse, straight leaf means a late picking. There is a protected origin, but the easiest check is simply where it was bought.

If you visit Hangzhou in spring for Longjing, buy a packet of this too: the same hills, the same picking standard, and a completely different tea.
sources_note: The Fujian-migrant origin story is the standard local account and is presented as such; cultivar mix is generalised from Hangzhou producers' descriptions.
